results.content:
Title: machine learning - Robustness vs Generalization - Data Science Stack Exchange
I don't quite understand the difference between robustness and generalisability in relation to image processing (CNN). If my model generalises well, it is also robust to changes in the image material. > The classic approach towards the assessment of any machine learning model revolves around the evaluation of its generalizability i.e. its performance on **unseen** test scenarios. > Evaluating such models on an available non-overlapping test set is popular, yet significantly limited in its ability to explore the model’s resilience to **outliers and noisy data** / labels (i.e. robustness). My approach to answering the question is in light of the language industry leaders are using like Google and Facebook in their open-source and published papers. Robustness as a term has been used by Google to refer to model performance on OOD (Out of Distribution) Data with Covariate or Subpopulation Shift [1]. Also in line with the previous answer, Facebook used Robustness to refer to model resilience to Adversarial Attacks [2]. Furthermore, Google to demo the robustness of their new model Pixel, 1- they presented the argument that it performs well on benchmark datasets of OOD and 2- on a colab notebook for plex\_vit computer vision model practical demo [4], they used adversarial attacks with adding gaussian noise on images to demo its reliance to it like Facebook in [2]. Robustness has also been described by Domain Adaptation by Facebook in their paper [5] where they measured Domain Adaptability by performance on OOD benchmarks datasets (Colored/Rotated MNIST, VLCS, PACS, Office-Home, Terra-Incognita, and DomainNet) much like Google did in [1] (except google called it Robustness). In conclusion, in image classification at least, I think robustness is a model's ability to classify objects it was trained to in the training set in a noisy/or-not-noisy (pictures could be clean) OOD test set. First, Domain Adaptation I think is a model's ability on learning classifying objects it was never trained on in the first place which is also google's description in [1]. However, Google refers to model performance on unseen test scenarios of the same data set as a special case of generalization called In-Distribution generalization [3]. performances evaluation of image classification with different distribution for train and test set.

results.title: Cross-Validation: Ensuring Model Robustness - Engineer's Planet
results.content: # Cross-Validation: Ensuring Model Robustness. In the ever-evolving landscape of machine learning, ensuring the robustness of models is paramount for reliable predictions. This involves evaluating a model’s performance under various conditions to validate its generalization capabilities beyond the training data. Cross-Validation: Ensuring Model Robustness emerges as a pivotal technique in achieving this goal. ### 1.2 Role of Cross-Validation. Cross-validation serves as a crucial tool for assessing model robustness by systematically partitioning data into training and testing sets. This process allows for a comprehensive evaluation of a model’s performance on different subsets, ensuring it can handle variations and generalize well. It guards against overfitting by providing a more accurate estimate of a model’s performance on unseen data, guiding practitioners in model selection and hyperparameter tuning. ### 2.1 k-Fold Cross-Validation. Cross-validation is a pivotal technique in machine learning that ensures the robustness of models by evaluating their performance on different subsets of data.

Title: Paper page - Validate on Sim, Detect on Real -- Model Selection for Domain

# Validate on Sim, Detect on Real -- Model Selection for Domain Randomization. A method called VSDR combines out-of-distribution detection with simulation evaluation to rank policies for sim2real transfer in robotics, improving accuracy and reducing real-world data usage. A practical approach to learning robot skills, often termed sim2real, is to. train control policies in simulation and then deploy them on a real robot. Popular techniques to improve the sim2real transfer build on domain. randomization (DR) -- training the policy on a diverse set of randomly. generated domains with the hope of better generalization to the real world. to the large number of hyper-parameters in both the policy learning and DR. algorithms, one often ends up with a large number of trained policies, where. choosing the best policy among them demands costly evaluation on the real. In this work we ask - can we rank the policies without running them in. Our main idea is that a predefined set of real world data can. be used to evaluate all policies, using out-of-distribution detection (OOD). policies before any real world execution. OOD score can be inaccurate and very sensitive to the particular OOD method. Our main contribution is a simple-yet-effective policy score that combines OOD. with an evaluation in simulation. We show that our score - VSDR - can. significantly improve the accuracy of policy ranking without requiring. We evaluate the effectiveness of VSDR on sim2real. different DR parameters and OOD methods, and show that VSDR improves policy. better ranking, and uses significantly less data compared to baselines. results.title: Domain Generalization Vs. ID-OOD Generalization Vs. Domain Adaptation Vs. Robustness Vs.Open-Set Recognition | by Emad Ezzeldin ,Sr. DataScientist@UnitedHealthGroup | Medium
results.content: Google in [2] describes Out-Of-Distribution generalization as possibly two of the four mentioned in Robust Generalization which are covariate and sub-population shifts. “In contrast to OOD generalization where the test example belongs to the same in-distribution training classes.” and also “In the real world, we care not only about metrics on new data obtained from the same distribution the model was trained on (i.i.d.), but also about robustness, as measured by metrics on data under out-of-distribution shifts such as covariate or subpopulation shift.” [2]. Facebook in [3] describes Domain Generalization as a classifier's ability to accurately predict samples from the same class but from a different data source as shown in the image below from [3]. Which is similar in description to google’s description of Out-Of-Domain Generalization, especially for Covariate Shift. Actually, Google in [1] gives an example of Covariate Shift, training on dog images, and predicting on dog drawings, which is similar to the nature of datasets Facebook used in [2]. **All in all, the Domain Generalization term used by Facebook in [3] and Out-of-Distribution Generalization used by Google in [1] and [2] are two terms describing the same quality for a model. Where most likely Facebook’s Domain Generalization just means generalization on Covariate Shifted data.**. Google in [1] defined Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Generalization by four types and describes a model’s ability to perform well on all four types as “Robust Generalization”. That implies that if a model is resilient to Adversarial Attacks, it will most likely also have good OOD Generalization on Covariate Shifted data. **So all in all, if a model is resilient to Adversarial attacks, it will be Robust to Spurious Correlations and it will have good OOD/Domain Generalization on Covariate Shifts.**. **All in all, the Domain Generalization term used by Facebook in [3] and Out-of-Distribution Generalization used by Google in [1] and [2] are two terms describing the same quality for a model. Where most likely Facebook’s Domain Generalization just means generalization on Covariate Shifted data. Also, if a model is resilient to Adversarial attacks, it will be Robust to Spurious Correlations and it will have good OOD/Domain Generalization on Covariate Shifts.**.
